title: Methamphetamine/amphetamine abuse and risk of Parkinson's disease in Utah: A population-based assessment

claims.statement: Whether methamphetamine use, as people use it, causes lasting loss of or damage to dopamine neurons in humans has not been established: lower dopamine markers in heavy users are consistently found, but the measures available cannot distinguish loss of nerve terminals from reversible down-regulation, some markers return toward normal with abstinence, and the pattern differs from that of Parkinson's disease.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable: no study has counted dopamine neurons or terminals quantitatively in human users.

claims.statement: In a Utah health-records cohort, people with a methamphetamine- or amphetamine-related diagnosis (n=4,935) received a later Parkinson's disease diagnosis code more often than matched controls (15 vs 27 events; HR 2.8, 95% CI 1.6–4.8), about 0.30% vs 0.11% over a mean 6.8 years; a California hospital cohort reported HR 1.76 (1.12–2.75). People with cocaine-related diagnoses showed no increase. In the Utah cohort the diagnoses came at a median age of 49, about 2 years after baseline, and few people received levodopa, so diagnostic misclassification and unadjusted smoking remain plausible explanations.
claims.magnitude: Utah: HR 2.8 (1.6–4.8), 15 vs 27 events; editors' absolute risks 0.30% vs 0.11% over mean 6.8 years (about 2 extra per 1,000); broader movement-disorder outcome HR 3.1 (30 vs 49 events). California: HR 1.76 (1.12–2.75) vs an appendicitis cohort (as reported by Kish et al., 2017; primary paper not yet read).
